places.role: Semiannual antiques fair created by Irene Stella of Stella Show Management in the passenger-ship terminals on Manhattan's Hudson River waterfront; at its "Triple Pier" peak it filled Piers 88, 90, and 92 with hundreds of dealers, ranking among New York City's largest antiques events. MSL browsed the show in a two-part field-trip segment.

places.name: Rhodes, Ragen & Smith
places.role: Seattle architectural-stone firm founded by master stonemason Richard Rhodes, who apprenticed in the ancient masons' guild of Siena, Italy; the company became known for reclaiming antique stone — including material from villages displaced by China's Three Gorges Dam — for American building projects, and continues today as Rhodes Architectural Stone. Featured in an MSL field-trip segment.

places.name: Nashville, Tennessee
places.role: Tennessee's capital and the heart of the American country-music industry — home of the Grand Ole Opry, the Ryman Auditorium, and Music Row — long nicknamed "Music City." Destination of an MSL field-trip episode that also featured nearby ham curer Ed Rice of Rice's Country Hams.

places.name: Gorham Silver
places.role: Founded in Providence, Rhode Island in 1831 by silversmith Jabez Gorham, the Gorham Manufacturing Company grew into the world's leading silverware maker by the 1860s, producing everything from coin-silver spoons and sterling flatware to monumental bronze casting. MSL profiled its Rhode Island factory in a segment on fine silver.

places.name: Viking Range
places.role: Greenwood, Mississippi appliance maker founded by fourth-generation builder Fred E. Carl Jr., who designed the first professional-grade range for home use — Viking's first ranges shipped in 1987 and launched the entire "pro-style" residential kitchen category. Featured in an MSL company segment.

places.name: South River Miso Company
places.role: Family-run maker of traditional wood-fired, unpasteurized organic miso, founded in 1982 by Christian and Gaella Elwell on a farm along the South River in Conway, Massachusetts. Beans and grains are cooked over wood fire in a timber-frame building warmed by a masonry stove, then aged in wooden vats — featured in an MSL segment (the rundown misspells it 'Southern River Miso').

places.name: Portland Classical Chinese Garden
places.role: Ming-dynasty-style walled garden in Portland, Oregon's Old Town Chinatown, built by 65 artisans from Portland's sister city Suzhou and opened in September 2000, only about two years before this MSL field trip. Renamed Lan Su Chinese Garden in 2010 — 'Lan' from Portland, 'Su' from Suzhou, poetically 'Garden of Awakening Orchids.'

places.name: Scalamandré
places.role: Luxury textile house founded in 1929 by Italian immigrant Franco Scalamandré and his designer wife Flora Baranzelli, who wove their first fine silks in a Long Island City, New York mill. Famed for passementerie — ornamental trimmings, tassels, and fringe — and for historic restorations from the Kennedy White House to Hearst Castle; MSL visited for a trimming segment.

places.name: SavATree
places.role: Tree, shrub, and lawn-care company headquartered in Bedford Hills, New York, founded in 1978 by Ralph Robbins to save Northeast trees from gypsy moth caterpillar defoliation; it grew into one of the country's largest arboriculture firms. MSL featured its arborists in a tree-safety training segment.

places.name: Pezzini Farms
places.role: Family farm in Castroville, California — the self-proclaimed Artichoke Center of the World — growing heirloom Green Globe artichokes from rootstock the Pezzini family brought from Italy in 1929. Its farm stand on Nashua Road just off Highway 1, opened in 1974, is beloved for fried artichoke hearts; visited for an MSL artichoke segment.

places.name: Gallup & Stribling Orchids
places.role: Orchid nursery established in 1954 in Carpinteria, California by horticulturist Aleck Stribling — who grew up on Montecito's orchid-laden Riven Rock estate — with father-and-son partners Emmet and Gary Gallup. It became the largest grower and distributor of cymbidium orchids in the United States, with roughly 48 acres of greenhouses; toured in a multi-part MSL field-trip segment.

places.name: Dorothy Timberlake Candies
places.role: Family candy kitchen in Eaton Center, New Hampshire that made old-fashioned molded barley candy from 1971 to 2009, casting lollipops and clear-toy candies from a collection of more than 13,000 antique molds. Dorothy Timberlake started the business after asking for candy molds for her birthday — the candy she remembered from childhood; featured in an MSL barley-candy segment.

places.name: Antique Rose Emporium
places.role: Nursery and display garden in Independence, Texas, near Brenham, founded in 1983 by horticulturist Mike Shoup, the 'Rose Rustler,' who propagated old garden roses rescued from abandoned homesteads and cemeteries. Its display gardens of time-tested antique varieties made it a pilgrimage site for rose lovers; visited in an MSL rose segment.

places.name: Monarch Watch
places.role: Education, conservation, and research program founded in 1992 by insect ecologist Orley 'Chip' Taylor at the University of Kansas. Its volunteer network of students, teachers, and citizen scientists has tagged millions of monarch butterflies to map the fall migration to the mountains of central Mexico; featured in an MSL segment.

places.name: San Antonio, TX
places.role: South Texas city that has been the American home of trabajo rústico — the Mexican faux bois concrete-sculpture tradition — since sculptor Dionicio Rodríguez arrived in 1924, leaving works that still dot Brackenridge Park. MSL came to town for a field-trip visit with Carlos Cortés, the tradition's third-generation master.

places.name: Sonoma, CA
places.role: Historic plaza town at the heart of Sonoma Valley wine country — site of Mission San Francisco Solano (1823), the last of California's Spanish missions, and of the 1846 Bear Flag Revolt, and a birthplace of California winemaking. The show opened an 'American Made' episode on location here during its final season.

places.name: Bahamas
places.role: Atlantic archipelago nation of some 700 islands and cays southeast of Florida. The Martha Stewart Weddings team staged Colin Van Dervort and Liz Wilks's destination wedding at the Sandals Emerald Bay resort on Great Exuma for the 2010 special Bayou to Bahamas.

places.name: Rosine Green Associates
places.role: Brookline, Massachusetts antiques- and art-restoration studio (founded 1970) whose craftsmen restore furniture, metalwork, paintings, and objets d'art; credited in an early-season MSL segment.

places.name: Greenwich Orchids
places.role: Orchid grower and floral boutique at 106 Mason Street in Greenwich, Connecticut, founded in 1981 by Ted and Wendy Siegel, who built their own greenhouses and supplied orchids to florists up and down the East Coast. Martha visited for an orchid segment that aired in January 1996.

places.name: Selody Sod Farm
places.role: The Selody family's turf-grass farm in Somerset County, New Jersey, cutting sod for New York landscapers since the 1930s. It is the family farm on which Ken Selody — the topiary specialist, Atlock Farm founder, and Martha Stewart contributing editor — was raised.

places.name: Breezy Hill Orchard
places.role: Hudson Valley apple orchard and cider mill in Staatsburg, New York (est. 1949), owned since the 1980s by Cornell-trained pomologist Elizabeth Ryan, the 'Grand Dame of Hudson Valley Cider.' Grows some 50 apple varieties and presses fresh and European-style ciders.

places.name: Penn & Fletcher
places.role: New York custom-embroidery atelier founded in 1986 by designers Andrew B. Marlay and Ernest A. Smith, one of the last embroidery houses in the city. Its workroom produces embroidered curtains, valances, and furnishings for Broadway, opera, film, museums, and top interior designers.

places.name: Belleclare Nursery
places.role: Legendary fig nursery in Plainview, Long Island, run for nearly 50 years by brothers Chris and Bill DiPaola, whose collection of rare Mediterranean fig varieties made 'Belleclare' figs prized by collectors to this day. The DiPaolas were among the most influential fig propagators in America.

places.name: Atlock Farm
places.role: Renowned seven-acre topiary nursery at 545 Weston Canal Road, Somerset, New Jersey, founded in 1987 by Ken Selody on a piece of his family's turf-grass farm. Selody — a former Martha Stewart contributing editor trained under topiary master Allen Haskell — made Atlock the East Coast's premier source for sculpted myrtle, rosemary, and coleus standards, with clients including Martha Stewart and the White House.

places.name: The Lobster Club
places.role: Chef Anne Rosenzweig's Upper East Side Manhattan restaurant (1995-2001), an American-comfort-food sequel to her acclaimed Arcadia, famous for its signature lobster club sandwich and upscale takes on homey dishes like the hamburger.

places.name: Charles H. Beckley, Inc.
places.role: Charles H. Beckley, Inc. is a South Bronx, New York custom mattress workshop founded in 1931, hand-making mattresses, box springs, headboards, and daybeds for the interior-design trade. Martha Stewart is a documented client — she ordered her own favorite firm mattresses and box springs from Beckley — and the company appeared on the Martha Stewart Living television program.

places.name: Patroon
places.role: Patroon (now Aretsky's Patroon) is restaurateur Ken Aretsky's clubby Midtown Manhattan restaurant at 160 East 46th Street, opened in 1995 and awarded three New York Times stars in the late 1990s under chef Franck Deletrain. Aretsky, a former '21' Club operator, has known Martha Stewart for decades and counts her among the restaurant's prominent regulars.

places.name: The Four Seasons Restaurant
places.role: Landmark Manhattan restaurant (1959-2019) in Philip Johnson-designed rooms inside Mies van der Rohe's Seagram Building at 99 East 52nd Street; birthplace of the 'power lunch', famed for menus that changed with the seasons and for its signature crisp duck. MSL devoted a full July 1998 episode to preparing its classic duck in four parts.

places.name: Cutchogue Fire Department Chicken Barbecue
places.role: Annual chicken barbecue held since the 1950s by the Cutchogue Fire Department and its Ladies Auxiliary in Cutchogue on Long Island's North Fork, cooking thousands of chickens over open pits with a famously secret basting sauce. Martha attended for a 1998 MSL episode, tried (unsuccessfully) to get the sauce recipe, and later hired the department to cater her company clambake.

places.name: Westport Digital Studios
places.role: A 1929 office-and-warehouse complex at 19 Newtown Turnpike in Westport, CT that Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia leased from 1998 to 2004 and converted into the show's television production home — three sound stages, a broadcast control room, two prep kitchens, and six wooded acres for outdoor filming, with Studio A's kitchen set modeled on Martha's East Hampton (Lily Pond Lane) kitchen. The September 1998 season-six opener toured the newly built facility in a 'Studio A Before & After' segment.

places.name: Prime Steakhouse (Bellagio, Las Vegas)
places.role: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's celebrated steakhouse overlooking the fountains at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas, opened with the resort in 1998 and long regarded as one of the city's premier fine-dining rooms. Martha's field-trip segments toured its potato and sauce work and steak presentation shortly after it opened.

places.name: Leonards New England
places.role: Antiques dealer in Seekonk, Massachusetts (founded 1933 by Lester and Hazel Leonard), famous for the country's largest collection of antique beds and for pioneering the resizing of antique bed frames to fit modern mattresses. Martha visited with owner Jeffrey Jenkins, who bought the family business in 1988, for the 'Leonards Beds' segment.

places.name: The Windsor Institute
places.role: Windsor chairmaking school in Hampton, New Hampshire, founded in 1994 by Mike Dunbar — the craftsman credited with reviving American Windsor chairmaking — and his wife Susanna. It taught five-day chair-building courses year-round until closing in 2016.

places.name: Betlan Corporation
places.role: Custom architectural fabrication shop in Ansonia, Connecticut, founded in 1985, known for bespoke metal countertops, range hoods, sinks, and cabinetry for high-end residential kitchens (its work has also appeared in This Old House idea houses).

places.name: Green Animals Topiary Garden
places.role: The oldest topiary garden in the United States, on a seven-acre estate in Portsmouth, Rhode Island, maintained by the Preservation Society of Newport County. Its more than 80 sculpted privet, yew, and boxwood figures — many shaped as animals — were created by gardeners Joseph Carreiro and George Mendonca over eight decades.

places.name: Frankoma Pottery
places.role: Oklahoma pottery company founded in 1933 by ceramicist John Frank and based in Sapulpa from 1938, famed for Southwestern-inspired dinnerware and art pottery made from local Ada and Sapulpa clay in signature glazes like Prairie Green and Desert Gold. Its wares became a sought-after mid-century collectible, and on Martha Stewart Living the collection was presented by MSL garden editor Margaret Roach, the collector who introduced Martha to Frankoma.

places.name: Shepaug Dam Bald Eagle Observation Area
places.role: Winter bald-eagle viewing site at the Shepaug hydroelectric dam on the Housatonic River in Southbury, Connecticut. Open December through early March since 1985, its volunteer-staffed observation blind overlooks the open water below the dam where wintering eagles gather to fish.

places.name: Flying Disc Ranch
places.role: Permaculture date farm in Thermal, California, in the heart of the Coachella Valley, founded in 1979 by former champion frisbee player Robert Lower. The roughly eleven-acre grove grows organic dates alongside citrus, figs, and pomegranates, and remains a farmers-market fixture across California.

places.name: Martha by Mail
places.role: Martha Stewart's own mail-order catalog and e-commerce business, launched in 1995 and folded into Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia's Internet/Direct Commerce division, selling exclusive housewares, craft kits, and baking tools until it wound down in 2004. MSL aired occasional behind-the-scenes segments on how its products were developed.

places.name: City Park (New Orleans)
places.role: New Orleans's 1,300-acre municipal park, founded in 1854, home to the world's largest collection of mature live oaks as well as the New Orleans Museum of Art and Botanical Garden. Visited as a field trip during the show's New Orleans episode.

places.name: Young Concert Artists
